title: Respiratory Protection Basics
summary: Dust, fumes, and other airborne contaminants on construction sites cause serious lung disease. Respirators only work when selected right, fit tested, and used under a written program. This talk covers controls first, then respirators.
talking_points: Control the hazard first: eliminate it, substitute a safer material, or use engineering controls like local exhaust ventilation and wet methods before relying on respirators.
When controls are not enough and exposures go above OSHA limits, respiratory protection is required.
Your employer must provide a NIOSH-approved respirator suited to the job. Check the approval label for the protection level, such as N95.
Use respirators under an OSHA-compliant program that includes medical evaluation, fit testing, and training.
Fit testing is required for tight-fitting respirators so they give the protection expected. Follow the manufacturer's instructions for putting them on and taking them off.
Inspect, maintain, and store respirators as the manufacturer directs. Replace filters and cartridges when they are damaged, soiled, hard to breathe through, or below the required airflow.
site_hazards_to_check: Dusty or fume-generating tasks with no wet method, ventilation, or other engineering control
Workers in respirators with no fit test, medical evaluation, or training on record
Wrong respirator or filter/cartridge type for the contaminant present
Damaged, soiled, or hard-to-breathe-through respirators and filters still in use
Respirators stored in dust, sun, or a dirty gang box
discussion_questions: What controls can cut the dust or fumes on this task before we reach for a respirator?
Has everyone using a tight-fitting respirator been fit tested for this model?
How do you know when a filter or cartridge needs to be replaced?

flags: OSHA mapping verified accurate: 29 CFR 1926.103 (construction respiratory protection, which adopts 1910.134) and 1910.134. Content correctly puts the hierarchy of controls first (eliminate/substitute/engineering controls before respirators), requires NIOSH-approved selection matched to the contaminant, and requires a written program with medical evaluation, fit testing for tight-fitting respirators, training, and maintenance/storage. No tolerance issues.
